title: Sorrel and the Invisible Ribbons
markdown:
Once upon a time, nestled among whispering pines and beneath skies painted with the soft hues of twilight, lived a young elf named Sorrel. Their days followed the gentle rhythm of Bramblehorn, as soothing as the brook that sang through the valley. They loved collecting smooth river-worn pebbles, each a miniature story, cool and polished in nimble fingers. They adored watching tiny fireflies wink secret messages in the gathering dusk, little lights like fallen stars dancing in the meadow. Thoughts drifted like dandelion fluff on the breeze until it was time to gather more dewdrops. A tiny flaw, like glitter on a forest floor, or a single misplaced feather in an otherwise perfect nest: they were easily, delightfully distracted by anything that sparkled. A dewdrop catching the sun. A beetle’s rainbow shell. A particularly shiny mushroom.

Every day they tidied their small moss-roofed home, ensuring not a single fallen leaf disrupted the cozy order. They gathered dewdrops for their morning drink—each drop a tiny prism holding a miniature world—in a delicate acorn cup. They practised a leaf-whistle so sweet and clear it could make the shyest forest flowers open a little wider, and coax shy rabbits from burrows. Bramblehorn was usually so predictable, so steady, like the slow sure growth of the ancient trees.

Until one day. Evening: the moon climbed like a silver berry. Forest lights, usually warm gold, flickered as if catching a cold. Path markers—cheerful ribbons of red, blue, and green tied to old oaks—were bare. Not a scrap left. A strange silence, only the nervous rustle of leaves.

Sorrel’s curiosity tingled, fizzy as lemonade. A puzzle, and the sparkle of the unknown outshone any gemstone. Pine-scented courage. They stepped onto the winding path after dusk.

A rumble like distant summer thunder. On a mossy boulder, a baby dragon no bigger than a badger, wings like dragonfly silk shifting colour, scales a freshly laundered rainbow. Large golden eyes, honey stirred by sunlight.

“H-hello?” Soft as a moth’s wing.

“Rumble,” said the dragon, a sound like a woolly blanket.

“I’m Sorrel. The path ribbons are gone. Have you seen them?”

A puff of smoke smelling of toasted marshmallows. “Flar,” it rumbled, and nodded toward the deeper woods. Glow-worms, usually blinking along the stream, dotted the path in a haphazard trail, winking with less cheer.

Sorrel stood still, listening. Friendly, like a very large purring cat.

They became a team, bound by the mystery. Sorrel, with keen elf eyes that could spot a lost berry from ten paces, followed the faint wobbling lights. Flar trotted faithfully beside them, low rumble vibrating through the mossy ground, rainbow wings catching dappled moonlight. The trail led deeper than Sorrel usually ventured, past ancient gnarled trees that seemed to whisper secrets, toward a small clearing bathed in the eerie glow of misplaced glow-worms.

They paused at the edge. The rumble. The sparks ahead. Then they stepped in.

A young wizard, brow furrowed like a ploughed field, spectacles sliding, midnight-blue robes letting out tiny sparks. Hands waving, muttering like fizzing lemonade and popping corn. Calista Buttonbright, whose magic was as eager as a puppy.

“Excuse me. We’re looking for missing path ribbons.”

Calista stopped mid-mutter. “Ribbons? I haven’t seen any. I am currently perfecting a brand-new, extremely advanced invisibility spell.” A proud gesture at empty air. “Everything I point at should, theoretically, disappear.”

A pale pulsing glow from fingertips. Flar’s questioning rumble. The glow-worms shrinking. Sorrel looked from hands to bare branches. The ribbons were not stolen. They were invisible: floating like Flar’s smoke, without marshmallow. The spell, meant for objects, was taking colour and fabric, sending ribbons away like forgotten wishes.

“Oh, Calista. Your spell is powerful. It seems to be working a little too well. Making the ribbons invisible, not just the objects you aim at. Like hiding a whole tree by only hiding its leaves.”

The sparks quieted. A berry blush. “I’ve been making things unseen when I meant to make them un-there? Like hiding a cake by vanishing the icing?”

“It seems so. Perhaps we can help you adjust it. Tricky as catching moonlight in a sieve.”

Flar rumbled agreement. Sorrel explained how a ribbon’s magic was tied to being seen, how colours told where it had been. Calista, humbled, concentrated not on disappearing but on making things truly themselves: shape, texture, essence.

Until finally, with a soft poof and a shower of harmless dust that smelled of wild lavender, the path ribbons reappeared, brighter than ever. Glow-worms sighed back to the stream. Forest lights settled, as after a bad dream. The spell would now hide a cookie from a squirrel, or a shy flower from a caterpillar—not an entire path-marker.

Calista’s sheepish smile. “Thank you, Sorrel. And Flar—you were a most excellent rumble-companion.”

Flar puffed marshmallow smoke. Rainbow wings gave a little flutter. They did not hurry the clearing. Ribbons stirred on their oaks, brighter and more colourful than ever. The air buzzed with a shared sense of accomplishment, warm as a freshly baked loaf. Then the three of them walked the marked way home, colours telling their stories again. Calista practised with better aim and a clearer sense of what invisible ought to mean. Flar’s rumble became a welcome sound in Bramblehorn, a sign of good luck. The oaks, for once, did not need to remember the tale aloud. The ribbons did it for them.
